opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, McKinsey was a really interesting experience, mostly because it showed me how much of getting things done is not about having the right answer. You come in thinking the hard part is the analysis: build the model, find the insight, put it on a slide. Then you realize the analysis is maybe twenty percent of it. The rest is figuring out who actually has to say yes, what they're worried about, and how to make the change feel like their idea rather than something imposed on them.

One thing that stuck with me is how much agency matters, and how rare it is. In a big organization there are endless reasons why something can't happen: it's not my remit, we need sign-off from this other team, we tried that three years ago. The people who really moved things were the ones who just assumed it could be done and kept pulling on threads until it was. Often they weren't the most senior people in the room. They were the ones willing to own the outcome end to end.

The other lesson was about the cost of coordination. A lot of what looks like inefficiency is really just the overhead of getting many people aligned, and that overhead grows faster than headcount. Small, tightly knit teams with a clear goal can move astonishingly fast compared to a large group with diffuse responsibility. That's partly why I find research labs so exciting. When you have a handful of people who deeply understand the problem and trust each other, you skip most of that friction.

And honestly, it taught me what I didn't want to do long term. I wanted to be closer to the actual thing being built rather than advising on it from the outside. But I'm grateful for it, because understanding how institutions actually work, the incentives and the politics, turns out to be useful almost everywhere, including in AI.

r001.rationale: It says impactful people assumed the work could be done and kept pulling on threads despite organizational obstacles.

r002.rationale: It links diffuse responsibility and people disclaiming remit to stalled work, and contrasts that with people owning the outcome end to end.

r003.rationale: The response does not say McKinsey provides temporary access to people organizations otherwise could not hire.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I was at McKinsey for a relatively short stint, and I think the honest answer is that it taught me less about how to get things done and more about how most things don't get done, and why.

The thing that struck me was how much of the work inside large organizations is essentially about information transfer and alignment rather than actual execution. You'd have these enormous companies with thousands of incredibly capable people, and the binding constraint was almost never talent or resources. It was that nobody quite had the full picture, and the people who had the authority to make a decision were often three or four layers removed from the people who actually understood the problem. So an enormous fraction of effort goes into just getting the right context in front of the right person at the right time.

And the corollary, which I think is actually the more useful lesson, is that a small number of people who genuinely understand something end to end can be dramatically more effective than a much larger group where that understanding is fragmented. You'd see it all the time. One person who'd actually gone and talked to the customers, looked at the data themselves, and could hold the whole thing in their head would just run circles around a committee.

The other thing it drilled into me was the value of being really crisp about what the actual question is. McKinsey is sometimes mocked for the frameworks and the slide decks, and fairly so in some cases, but the underlying discipline of forcing yourself to state the problem precisely, figure out what would change your mind, and then go get exactly that evidence, that's genuinely useful. A lot of smart people spend a lot of time doing work that's interesting but doesn't actually move the decision.

I think both of those ended up being pretty relevant when I moved into AI research. The projects that go well tend to have a tight group of people with shared context and a very clear sense of what question they're trying to answer. And the ones that stall tend to have exactly the organizational pathologies I saw consulting, just with better compute budgets.

r001.rationale: The response discusses information transfer, alignment, and precise problem definition, but does not identify refusing to take no for an answer as a source of organizational impact.

r002.rationale: It says decision-makers can be removed from people who understand the problem, but does not identify lack of individual ownership as a cause of work failing to get done.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention McKinsey providing temporary access to people organizations could not otherwise hire.

astra-6.text:
The biggest lesson was that knowing what should happen and getting it to happen are quite different problems. You can have a sensible recommendation, but somebody has to take responsibility for it, persuade the people whose work will change, and keep pushing when it runs into friction.

It also made me appreciate how much context people inside an organization have. Something can look obviously inefficient from the outside, and then you discover that it exists because of a constraint you didn’t understand. That doesn’t mean you should accept it. It means you need to understand what problem it was solving before you replace it.

So I came away paying more attention to ownership and feedback: who can actually make the decision, who will do the work, and how quickly will they find out whether it worked?

r001.rationale: It says to keep pushing through friction, but does not identify refusing to take no for an answer as a source of organizational impact.

r002.rationale: It connects getting work done to someone taking responsibility and emphasizes ownership, communicating that work can fail without individual ownership.

r003.rationale: It does not mention McKinsey providing temporary access to people organizations could not otherwise hire.

sol-6.1.text:
The biggest lesson was that being right and getting something to happen are quite different skills. You can do a great analysis, but unless someone inside the organization understands it, believes it, and has the authority to act on it, nothing changes.

From the outside, you imagine a company as this coherent entity pursuing a goal. Inside, it’s people with different incentives, different information, and different things they’re worried about. A lot of getting things done is understanding those constraints and finding someone who will actually own the decision.

It also made me appreciate how much a motivated individual can matter. Sometimes what looks like an organizational capability is really one person who keeps pushing, follows up, and makes sure the gaps between teams get filled.

r001.rationale: The response says a motivated individual may keep pushing and follow up, but does not clearly identify refusing to take no for an answer as the source of impact.

r002.rationale: It says nothing changes unless someone has authority to act and that getting things done involves finding someone to own the decision.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention McKinsey giving organizations temporary access to people they could not otherwise hire.
